findings.finding: My current finding is that any α with exactly one non‑zero entry equal to ±1 (and zero elsewhere on {0,…,8}) is shifty: choose any distinct integers k,l, set β(k)=β(l)=±1 at the positions j=i−k and j=i−l, then Sₙ(α)⋆β=1 precisely for n=k,l and 0 otherwise. Hence there are 9·2 = 18 such α. This already shows that at least 18 shifty functions exist.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a Laurent polynomial  

\[
A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}a_i z^i\qquad(a_i\in\mathbb Z)
\]

that, up to a unit ± z^s, is a divisor (in ℤ[z]) of a binomial \(1+z^d\) for some integer \(d>0\).  Indeed, writing β’s shifted version γ(z)=∑β(−t)z^t, the condition \(S_n(α)\starβ=δ_{k}+δ_{l}\) becomes  

\[
A(z)\,B(z)=z^{k}+z^{l}=z^{\min(k,l)}\bigl(1+z^{|k-l|}\bigr),
\]

so \(A(z)=\pm z^{s}D(z)\) where \(D(z)\mid(1+z^{d})\).  Consequently every admissible α is a shift of a product of distinct cyclotomic factors Φ_{2m} (with m odd), i.e. a square‑free divisor of some \(1+z^{d}\).  This reduction to “α is a shifted divisor of \(1+z^{d}\)” is the key step for counting shifty functions.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a polynomial \(A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)z^{i}\) that divides a binomial \(z^{m}+1\) (with \(m\neq0\)) in the Laurent‑polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[z,z^{-1}]\); equivalently \(A(z)=\pm z^{c}D(z)\) where \(c\ge0\) and \(D(z)\) is an integer‑coefficient divisor of \(z^{m}+1\) for some non‑zero \(m\). This reduction shows the problem is purely about integer divisors of binomials, not about arbitrary β.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a primitive integer polynomial A(x)=∑_{i=0}^8α(i)x^i (deg ≤ 8) for which there exist integers d>0 and r≥0 such that  

\[
A(x)=x^{\,r}f(x),\qquad f(x)\mid (1+x^{d})\text{ in }\mathbb Z[x],
\]

i.e. f(x) is a divisor (with constant term ±1) of the binomial 1+x^d.  Because the product A·D must equal 1+x^d for some Laurent polynomial D, A must be primitive (gcd of its coefficients = 1) and its degree satisfies r+deg f ≤ 8.  Thus counting shifty functions reduces to counting all primitive factors f of 1+x^d (for any d) whose degree ≤ 8, together with all possible shifts r that keep the total degree ≤ 8.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a Laurent‑polynomial A(z)=±z^s·D(z) where D(z) is a divisor (in ℤ[z]) of a binomial 1+z^d.  Hence D(z) must be a product of distinct cyclotomic polynomials Φ_{2m} with m odd, and the degree of D must be ≤8 (because after the shift the support must lie in {0,…,8}).  The only such cyclotomics are  

\[
\Phi_2,\;\Phi_6,\;\Phi_{10},\;\Phi_{14},\;\Phi_{18},\;\Phi_{30}
\]

with degrees 1,2,4,6,6,8.  Enumerating all subsets whose total degree ≤8 gives 15 possible D’s (including the empty product 1).  For a divisor of degree δ, the shift s can be any integer 0≤s≤8−δ, giving 9−δ choices, and the overall sign gives a factor 2.  Summing \(2(9-δ)\) over the 15 subsets yields  

\[
\sum_{D}2(9-\deg D)=114.
\]

Thus there are **114** shifty functions in ℱ.  (All such α arise from the described construction, and no other α can satisfy the condition because any α must divide a binomial z^k+z^l.)

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a polynomial A(x)=∑_{i=0}^8α(i)x^i that can be written as  

\[
A(x)=x^{r}\,f(x),\qquad 0\le r\le 8-\deg f,
\]

where f(x) is a product of distinct cyclotomic polynomials Φ_{2^{v+1}t} whose indices all have the same 2‑adic exponent v+1 (v∈{0,1,2,3}) and whose odd parts t satisfy  

\[
\sum_{t\in T}2^{v}\varphi(t)\le8 .
\]

Thus f is a divisor of some x^{d}+1 (d=2^{v}·m) and must be primitive (content 1). The degree of α is deg A= r+∑_{t∈T}2^{v}\varphi(t). Consequently the total number of shifty functions equals  

\[
\sum_{f}\;2\bigl(9-\deg f\bigr),
\]

where the sum runs over all such f (including f=1). This reduces the original problem to enumerating all subsets T of odd t with the weighted‑totient bound above.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a polynomial  

\[
A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)z^{i}\in\mathbb Z[z]
\]

that divides a binomial \(z^{k}+z^{\ell}\) in the Laurent‑polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[z,z^{-1}]\).  Equivalently, after cancelling the monomial factor, \(A(z)=\pm z^{c}D(z)\) where \(D(z)\) is a product of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{n}(z)\) with even index \(n\) and total degree \(\le8\).  Moreover all \(\Phi_{n}\) appearing in a given \(D\) must share the same exact power of 2 in their index, i.e.  

\[
n\in\{2,6,10,14,18,30\}\;(2\text{-part}=2),\;
\{4,12,20\}\;(2\text{-part}=4),\;
\{8,24\}\;(2\text{-part}=8),\;
\{16\}\;(2\text{-part}=16).
\]

Thus every shifty α is obtained by choosing any subset of one of these four groups whose total degree ≤8, then shifting it by a monomial \(z^{c}\) with \(0\le c\le8-\deg D\) and optionally multiplying by \(-1\).  The total number of shifty functions will be  

\[
{2\sum_{D}(9-\deg D)},
\]

where the sum runs over all such products \(D\) (including the empty product).  This reduction replaces the original functional condition by a finite combinatorial enumeration of allowable cyclotomic‑factor subsets.

My current finding is that the “shifty’’ functions are **exactly** the integer‑valued functions whose generating polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}
\]

is a monomial \(x^{r}\) (giving a single non‑zero entry \(\pm1\) at some \(r\in\{0,\dots ,8\}\)) **or** a monomial times a divisor of a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) (with \(d\ge1\)).  In particular, besides the 18 functions with a single \(\pm1\) entry, any divisor of \(1+x^{d}\) whose degree \(\le8\) yields a shifty function.  For example, \(A(x)=1-x+x^{2}\) (coefficients \(1,-1,1\) at positions \(0,1,2\)) works with \(\beta\) supported at \(0\) and \(-1\), giving \(S_{n}(\alpha)\star\beta=1\) exactly for \(n=-1,2\).  Thus shifty functions are not limited to support size \(\le2\); they include all polynomials of the form \(x^{r}f(x)\) where \(f(x)\mid(1+x^{d})\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\) and \(\deg(x^{r}f)\le8\).

My current finding is that a shifty function \(\alpha\) must correspond to a Laurent polynomial \(A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)z^{i}\) which divides a binomial \(z^{k}+z^{\ell}=z^{k}(1+z^{d})\) in \(\mathbb Z[z,z^{-1}]\).  Hence, after factoring out a monomial unit, \(A(z)=\pm z^{s}D(z)\) where \(D(z)\) is a divisor of \(1+z^{d}\).  The only irreducible divisors of any \(1+z^{d}\) are cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{2m}(z)\) with \(m\) odd; for \(\deg D\le8\) the possible \(m\) are \(1,3,5,7,9,15\).  Thus \(D(z)\) is any square‑free product of the six cyclotomics \(\Phi_{2},\Phi_{6},\Phi_{10},\Phi_{14},\Phi_{18},\Phi_{30}\) whose total degree \(\le8\).  There are exactly 15 such products (including the empty product).  For each product of degree \(d\) we may shift it by any \(s\in\{0,\dots,8-d\}\) and choose either sign, giving \(2(9-d)\) distinct \(\alpha\).  Summing over the 15 possibilities yields  

\[
\sum_{D}2(9-\deg D)=114 .
\]

Therefore **the number of shifty functions in \(\mathcal F\) is \({114}\).**

My current finding is that a shifty function \(\alpha\) must satisfy  

\[
A(x)\,D(x)=1+x^{d},
\qquad A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i},
\]

where \(D(x)\) is a Laurent polynomial with integer coefficients and \(d>0\).  
Thus \(A(x)\) is a **primitive divisor** (content = 1) of a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) and its non‑zero coefficients lie in \([0,8]\).  

All such divisors are exactly the products of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{2^{v+1}t}\) with \(v\in\{0,1,2,3\}\) and odd \(t\) satisfying \(2^{v}\varphi(t)\le8\).  
Enumerating these gives 22 distinct monic polynomials \(f(x)\) (including \(f=1\)) with degrees \(\le8\).  

For each \(f\) of degree \(d_f\) we may shift it by any \(r\in\{0,\dots,8-d_f\}\) and change its sign, giving \(2\,(9-d_f)\) shifty functions.  

Summing over the 22 polynomials yields  

\[
\sum_{f}2\,(9-\deg f)=2\cdot80=160 .
\]

Hence **the number of shifty functions in \(\mathcal F\) is \({160}\).**

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a polynomial  

\[
A(z)=\pm z^{c}D(z),\qquad 0\le c\le 8-\deg D,
\]

where \(D(z)\) is a product of distinct **even‑indexed cyclotomic polynomials** \(\Phi_n(z)\) that all have the same 2‑adic exponent (i.e. \(n=2^{t+1}d\) with the same \(t\)).  Moreover \(\deg D\le8\).  Enumerating all such \(D\) gives 22 distinct polynomials (including \(1\)), with degrees  

\[
0,1,2,2,3,4,4,4,5,6,6,6,6,7,7,7,8,8,8,8,8,8 .
\]

For each \(D\) there are \(9-\deg D\) possible shifts \(c\) and two sign choices, so the total number of shifty functions is  

\[
2\sum_{D}(9-\deg D)=2\cdot80= {160}.
\]

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\pm x^{r}\,f(x),\qquad r\ge0,\;r+\deg f\le8,
\]

where \(f(x)\) is any (monic) divisor of a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) for some \(d\ge1\).  Equivalently, \(f\) is any product of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{2t}(x)\) (the even‑indexed cyclotomics); every such \(f\) divides \(1+x^{\operatorname{lcm}(t)}\).  Thus the number of shifty functions equals  

\[
\sum_{f}\bigl(8-\deg f+1\bigr)\times2,
\]

the sum ranging over all distinct products \(f\) of even cyclotomics (including the trivial factor \(f=1\)).  This reduces the counting problem to enumerating all such \(f\) with degree \(\le8\).

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a Laurent polynomial  

\[
A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)z^{i}
\]

that, up to a unit ± z^{s}, divides a binomial \(1+z^{d}\).  Hence  

\[
A(z)=\pm z^{s}\prod_{m\mid d,\;m\text{ odd}}\Phi_{2m}(z),
\]

where each cyclotomic factor \(\Phi_{2m}\) appears at most once.  Because \(\alpha\) is zero outside \([0,8]\), the total degree \(\delta=\sum\phi(m)\) of the product must satisfy \(\delta\le8\).  The only odd \(m\) with \(\phi(m)\le8\) are  

\[
m\in\{1,3,5,7,9,15\},
\]

giving cyclotomics \(\Phi_{2},\Phi_{6},\Phi_{10},\Phi_{14},\Phi_{18},\Phi_{30}\) of degrees \(1,2,4,6,6,8\).  Enumerating all subsets of these six with total degree \(\le8\) yields 15 possible products \(D(z)\).  For a product of degree \(\delta\) the shift \(s\) can be any integer \(0\le s\le8-\delta\) (giving \(9-\delta\) choices) and the overall sign gives a factor 2.  Summing \(2(9-\delta)\) over the 15 subsets gives  

\[
\sum_{D}2(9-\deg D)=114.
\]

Thus **there are exactly 114 shifty functions**.  Any answer different from 114 (e.g. 90 or 160) counts functions that either exceed the degree bound or are not divisors of a binomial, and therefore cannot satisfy the required convolution condition.

My current finding is that the only shifty functions are exactly the signed, shifted copies of the 22 primitive divisors \(f(x)\) of some binomial \(1+x^{d}\) with total degree \(\le8\); these divisors are precisely the products of distinct cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{2^{v+1}t}\) whose indices share the same 2‑adic exponent \(v+1\) (with \(v=0,1,2,3\)) and whose odd parts \(t\) satisfy \(\sum_{t}2^{v}\varphi(t)\le8\).  There are 22 such monic \(f\) (including \(f=1\)).  For each \(f\) of degree \(d_f\) we may shift by any \(r\) with \(0\le r\le8-d_f\) (giving \(9-d_f\) possibilities) and choose an overall sign, yielding \(2(9-d_f)\) shifty functions per \(f\).  Summing \(2(9-d_f)\) over the 22 divisors gives  

\[
\sum_{f}2(9-\deg f)=160.
\]

Thus the answer is \({160}\); the counts 90 and 114 cannot be correct because they omit many admissible cyclotomic‑factor subsets (e.g. \(x^6-2x^5+3x^4-3x^3+3x^2-2x+1\) of degree 6) that are accounted for in the above classification.

grouped by the common 2‑adic exponent.  Taking all subsets of each group whose total degree ≤ 8 yields exactly 22 distinct \(D\)’s (including \(D=1\)).  For each \(D\) there are \(9-\deg D\) possible shifts \(c\) and two sign choices, giving  

\[
\sum_{D}(9-\deg D)=80\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\#\text{shifty}=2\cdot80=160.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to an integer polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\pm x^{r}\prod_{t\in S}\Phi_{2t}(x)
\]

where each \(\Phi_{2t}\) is a cyclotomic polynomial of even index (the factors of \(1+x^{d}\)), the set \(S\) is any subset of

\Phi_{14},\Phi_{16},\Phi_{18},\Phi_{20},\Phi_{24},\Phi_{30}\,\},

and the total degree \(d_f=\sum_{t\in S}\deg\Phi_{2t}\) satisfies \(d_f\le8\); the shift exponent \(r\) can be any integer with \(0\le r\le8-d_f\).  

Counting all subsets with total degree ≤ 8 gives 266 distinct \(\alpha\)’s (each with two sign choices). Hence the number of shifty functions in \(\mathcal F\) is **266**.

shifty functions.  This matches the answers 160 from Solver 1 and Solver 3 and shows the 114 count is incomplete.

\]

for some integer \(d>0\).  Consequently every irreducible factor of \(f\) must be a cyclotomic polynomial \(\Phi_{n}(x)\) with even index \(n\), and all those indices must have the same 2‑adic exponent. My current finding is that a function α is shifty **iff** its generating polynomial A(x)=∑_{i=0}^8α(i)x^i can be written as  

\[
A(x)=\pm x^{r}\prod_{t\in S}\Phi_{2t}(x),
\]

where Φ_{2t} is the cyclotomic polynomial of order 2t, S is any set of positive integers with ∑_{t∈S}φ(2t)≤8, and 0≤r≤8−∑_{t∈S}φ(2t).  

Indeed, for such α let d=lcm(S) (or any d>0 if S=∅); then  

\[
1+x^{d}=\Bigl(\prod_{t\in S}\Phi_{2t}(x)\Bigr)\Bigl(\prod_{t\mid d,\;t\notin S}\Phi_{2t}(x)\Bigr),
\]

so choosing β with generating polynomial B(x^{-1})=±x^{r}\prod_{t\mid d,\;t\notin S}\Phi_{2t}(x) gives  

\[
A(x)B(x^{-1})=x^{r}(1+x^{d})=x^{k}+x^{\ell},
\]

hence S_n(α)⋆β equals 1 exactly at n=k,ℓ.  

Conversely, if α is shifty, the relation A(x)B(x^{-1})=x^{k}+x^{\ell} forces A(x) to divide a binomial x^{p}+x^{q}, so A(x) must be a product of such cyclotomic factors.  

Counting all subsets S with total degree ≤8 (there are 12 possible Φ_{2t} with degree ≤8) gives  

\[
\sum_{S}2\bigl(9-\sum_{t\in S}\varphi(2t)\bigr)=266.
\]

Thus **there are exactly 266 shifty functions**.

where each \(\Phi_{n}\) is a cyclotomic polynomial with even index \(n\) and \(\deg\Phi_{n}\le8\); the product runs over a subset \(S\) of the even indices  

\[

\]

\[
\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq\{2,\dots,30\}\\\delta\le8}}2\,(9-\delta)={266}.
\]

(There are 44 admissible subsets \(S\); their contributions sum to 266.) This shows the earlier answer 114 (which omitted the cyclotomics with index 4,8,12,16,20,24) and the answer 160 are both too small.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds to a Laurent polynomial  

\[
A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)z^{i}
\]

that, up to a sign, is a monomial \(z^{s}\) times a divisor \(D(z)\) of a binomial \(1+z^{d}\).  
All divisors of \(1+z^{d}\) are products of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{n}\) with even index \(n\); for a fixed \(d=2^{v}m\) (m odd) the factors are exactly those \(\Phi_{2^{v+1}t}\) with odd \(t\mid m\). Hence the cyclotomic factors that can appear must all have the same 2‑adic exponent \(v+1\).

The even‑indexed cyclotomics with degree \(\le8\) are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
v=0:&\ \{\,\Phi_{2},\Phi_{6},\Phi_{10},\Phi_{14},\Phi_{18},\Phi_{30}\,\},\\
v=1:&\ \{\,\Phi_{4},\Phi_{12},\Phi_{20}\,\},\\
v=2:&\ \{\,\Phi_{8},\Phi_{24}\,\},\\
v=3:&\ \{\,\Phi_{16}\,\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

A divisor \(D\) is any product of a **single‑v** subset of these, with total degree \(\delta\le8\).  
For each such \(D\) there are \(9-\delta\) possible shifts \(s\) (so that the support stays in \(\{0,\dots,8\}\)) and two signs, giving \(2(9-\delta)\) distinct α.

Summing over all admissible subsets (the empty set counted once) yields  

\[
\sum_{D}2(9-\deg D)=160.
\]

Thus the correct number of shifty functions is **160**, and the earlier answer 114 is too small because it omitted the cyclotomic factors with higher 2‑adic exponent (e.g. \(\Phi_{4},\Phi_{8},\Phi_{12},\Phi_{16},\Phi_{20},\Phi_{24}\)).
